item.title: Duffy Offers New Details on How One Fix Spiraled Into Nationwide Ground Stop
item.description:
The cascade of failures that led to the grounding of U.S. air traffic on Friday began with what officials say was supposed to be a routine router upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Ark. The station was remote enough, they figured, that they could do the work without causing undue harm.

But that swiftly proved to be a gross miscalculation.

The effort to upgrade the Federal Aviation Administration’s antiquated copper-wire-based system to fiber optic cable in Arkansas occurred as the agency officials noticed a second issue with a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas, where such work had been done weeks before, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday morning during a blitz of appearances across network and cable television.

Officials took the two facilities offline shortly after, but not before each had pinged the network with an abnormally high rate of connections. That prompted failures in other parts of the air traffic communications network that forced officials to declare a rare nationwide ground stop, Rebecca Guy, the F.A.A.’s chief technology officer, told reporters on Saturday.

But agency investigators still have not determined whether a faulty part or an error on the part of L3Harris, which owns the telecoms system in question and is responsible for upgrading and maintaining it, caused the initial problem in Arkansas. And Mr. Duffy said they are equally unsure why the facility in Amarillo failed on Friday when no upgrade work was being done there at the time.

The protracted crisis, from which airlines have yet to recover, and the lack of clarity from Trump administration officials about why things went wrong, have revived questions about whether the F.A.A. is equipped to carry out its plan for modernization without creating more risks for the nation’s air traffic control system.

The crisis has also heightened concerns about durability and the lack of backups in the nation’s critical air traffic infrastructure, if a failure at one small facility is enough to bring the functionality of the entire network down.

During an interview Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” Mr. Duffy said he could not guarantee that a meltdown like Friday’s would not happen again.

“First we have to figure out what happened,” he said, adding, “We’re going to figure out what was the root cause and then move forward from there, fixing how we do business at the F.A.A.”

He also deflected when asked if he was ultimately responsible for the meltdown and owed air passengers an apology.

“I can’t apologize for what was passed on to us,” he said, accusing prior administrations of having failed to tackle known infrastructure problems.

“I don’t apologize for shutting down the airspace and keeping people safe,” he added.

Skepticism surrounding how the F.A.A. has been carrying out its air traffic modernization plan is not new.

In September, the Government Accountability Office, a nonpartisan watchdog agency, issued a report raising concerns that the F.A.A. was in danger of “prioritizing speed over costs and air traffic disruptions” as it pursued its modernization plan. The report also criticized the agency for not having coordinated the schedules of 11,389 upgrade projects and not having conducted life-cycle cost estimates of existing technology, noting that “without them, the agency could end up causing air traffic disruptions or prolonging reliance on severely outdated systems.”

But such questions are especially pertinent since Mr. Duffy chose to seize on Friday’s meltdown by demanding that Congress give him $50 billion in new funding for air traffic control upgrades by the end of the year. That is a drastically larger sum than he has asked for before — and one that many lawmakers say he has not shown he would responsibly spend.

“It’s really rich to hear the secretary pointing the fingers at Congress when Congress has given the administration what they asked for,” Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat running to become majority leader, said on CNN’s “State of the Union.” “If they need more, they should come up and justify it.”

On Saturday, the White House put its weight behind Mr. Duffy’s ballooning demand for funding, and on Sunday, President Trump weighed in on social media to claim that his administration could build the “BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the world,” urging Congress “to give the money, FAST!”

But Mr. Trump dedicated more of his attention to blasting the Biden administration for the F.A.A.’s air traffic infrastructure problems than detailing what $50 billion more would pay for.

Mr. Duffy also has yet to itemize his $50 billion request. For several weeks, he has been calling for a $30 billion influx in F.A.A. funding, but only about $10 billion of that request was specifically for air traffic modernization. Another $10 billion of the funds was envisioned for airport beautification, and the last $10 billion for improvement projects at towers, terminals and airports.

Last year, Congress appropriated $12.5 billion for air traffic modernization, nearly two-thirds of which lawmakers dedicated for telecoms upgrades and radar replacements.

On Saturday, Bryan Bedford, the F.A.A. administrator, told reporters that his agency would need “about $10.1 billion to finish modernization,” on top of the $12.5 billion Congress already appropriated.

On Sunday, Mr. Duffy said that while the money his department has requested will go to pay for needed radio and radar upgrades, it will not cover all the costs of upgrading a telecom system reliant in some places on 1980s wiring and routers from 2001 that have long been obsolete.

“What I don’t have money for is the new telecoms system; I don’t have money for new software,” Mr. Duffy said on CBS’s “Face the Nation.” “Those are critical pieces to the new infrastructure and it’s been historically underinvested in.”

item.title: Van Hollen Says His Senate Challenge to Schumer Is Gaining Support
item.description:
Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat, contended on Sunday that he has a “wide open” path to unseat Senator Chuck Schumer of New York to become majority leader next year, intensifying the internal leadership battle that is dividing the newly empowered Democratic caucus.

Mr. Van Hollen, who has positioned himself as a populist underdog, said he did not believe Mr. Schumer’s support was solid. Mr. Schumer, an architect and funder of the successful Democratic effort to retake the Senate, has announced that he has locked up enough commitments to return him to the position of leader for another two years.

“I can tell you that a number of those people on that list have actually committed to voting for me,” Mr. Van Hollen said on CNN’s “State Of The Union,” though it was not clear what list he was referring to. “The others are very open to the idea of change.”

Mr. Van Hollen had previously said he had more than 10 colleagues supporting him.

On Sunday, he said on “Fox News Sunday” that number was up to 15 and growing. “This is a wide-open race,” he said.

The winner needs a simple majority of the caucus to vote for him in a secret-ballot election that is scheduled for Dec. 1. Democrats will make up at least 55 seats in the Senate next year, including the independents who caucus with them.

Mr. Van Hollen, 67, also accused Mr. Schumer, 75, who has led Senate Democrats since 2016, of trying to change that date because he was not confident he had the votes.

“If they really believed that they were ahead, they wouldn’t be trying to move up the elections,” Mr. Van Hollen, who appeared on three different programs on Sunday morning, said on Fox News. “They’re talking about trying to short-circuit that open debate process within the Democratic caucus.”

While there has been an internal discussion by some lawmakers of moving up the date of the election to avoid a prolonged internal battle, it is not clear that the idea has gained any traction and is not being driven by Mr. Schumer himself, people familiar with the conversations said.

Mr. Van Hollen said that he differed from Mr. Schumer in his position on funding the war with Iran. He said Congress should give “not one penny more” to fund the war, using the leverage of a government shutdown next month to force the issue. Congress has a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government to avoid a shutdown.

Mr. Schumer and other top Democrats have been weighing a temporary extension of government funding with some restrictions on the military money until early 2027, when they would hold the majority and likely be able to exert more leverage against the Trump administration.

Mr. Van Hollen also said he disagreed with Mr. Schumer’s decision to try to influence Democratic primaries during the midterm elections, particularly against Senators-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota.

“He joined with AIPAC and crypto to try and defeat them,” he said, referring to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which spent about $30 million in the competitive Michigan primary against Mr. El-Sayed.

While Mr. Schumer has been criticized for supporting some center-leaning candidates in primaries who ultimately lost to progressives, his allies noted that he recruited five winning candidates in states that Democrats flipped or are on track to do so: Mary Peltola in Alaska, Roy Cooper in North Carolina, Josh Turek in Iowa, Sherrod Brown in Ohio and Scott Colom in Mississippi.

They also noted that Senate Democrats’ campaign arm never spent money in the Minnesota Senate race.

Overall, though, Mr. Van Hollen said he was challenging Mr. Schumer because the message of the midterm elections was that the American people wanted change.

“We need to earn people’s trust, and I don’t think you do that by simply going back to business as usual,” Mr. Van Hollen said on Fox News.

item.title: Flight Delays and Cancellations Persist as Air Traffic System Recovers
item.description:
Air traffic operations over the United States continued to improve on Sunday after nearly all flights were grounded for more than 4 hours on Friday. Still, disruptions remained across the system with many flights canceled or delayed.

Nearly 90 percent of all flights left within 14 minutes of their scheduled departure time on Sunday morning, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company. But some 5 percent of flights — more than 1,300 trips — had already been canceled, higher than a typical day, showing the continuing effects of the nationwide flight freeze.

Disruptions have occurred at major hubs — from Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport in Georgia to Dallas Fort Worth International Airport in Texas — and at airports in Phoenix and Philadelphia.

The disruptions postponed college sports games and stranded professional basketball teams. Passengers slept overnight in airports and competed to rebook their flights; some canceled their trips entirely.

The logjam is the latest example of the vulnerabilities in the American air traffic system, which is facing twin crises: a shortage of air traffic controllers and an outdated infrastructure.

It was an upgrade to the system that officials have identified as the root cause of the problems that led to the shutdown on Friday. As the contractor L3 Harris was upgrading copper wires to fiber-optic cables, a router overloaded the system with data requests, disrupting communications.

As a result, tens of thousands of passengers endured a nightmare travel weekend. Some 9,000 flights were canceled on Friday, according to Cirium, while about 30 percent were delayed. As airlines worked to get back on track on Saturday, there were still 6,649 cancellations and more than half of all flights were delayed.

“Our air traffic control system is operating on DECADES-OLD, analog equipment that simply cannot compete with the demands of the 21st century,” Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, wrote on social media.

Officials said Sunday that they expected schedules to return to normal by late in the day or Monday morning.

For Ashley Greiner, 45, the delays have compounded.

On Saturday, her flight from Seattle to Atlanta was rerouted to Charlotte, N.C. But her connection to Atlanta was canceled, and she spent the night in North Carolina. On Sunday, she faced two delays and a plane change.

“I’m a heart-failure patient, and my trips were for speaking engagements to share my story with health care providers,” she said in a direct-message conversation. “This has been exceptionally hard on my body.”

The disruption in the communication system forced officials at the Federal Aviation Administration to ground flights at around 4 p.m. on Friday.

It was the third such ground stop this century.

Some 3,500 planes were airborne when the order went out, Secretary Duffy said on Friday.

Overall, more than 17,000 flights have been canceled since Friday, according to Cirium’s latest tally. Nearly 40 percent of the 74,696 scheduled flights since Friday have been delayed.

On Sunday, Secretary Duffy said the affected facilities in Texas and Arkansas were “secured” and diagnostic testing was underway.

“We have no indication of a foreign cyberattack, and we will continue to investigate alongside the F.B.I. and our federal law enforcement partners,” he said.

Brenda Folkerts, 59, arrived in New Orleans on Thursday for a marathon but now faces the prospect of a long trip to her home state of Washington on sore and tired legs. Her connection through Dallas was delayed by two hours on Sunday, and she missed her flight to Seattle. She does not know when or how she’ll make it home.

“My case is not unique,” she said in a direct message as her plane taxied. “Most people here have missed connections and are scrambling to figure out what to do.”

item.title: 8 Takeaways From a Big Democratic Gathering in Denver: Democrats in Array
item.description:
Democratic spirits were higher than the altitude in Denver, where more than 3,000 party strategists, activists, lawmakers and potential presidential candidates gathered last week to strategize how the party could capitalize on its dominant showing in the midterm elections.

Democrats flipped at least eight Senate seats while also securing what could be the largest House majority in a national election for either party in three decades.

“America is back,” Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the speaker-in-waiting, beamed at one welcome party.

For a party that is often fractious, there seemed little discord in Denver. Some of the loudest jeering over the three-day event came when the lights at the Ritz-Carlton hotel bar brightened and hundreds of drinking Democrats booed in unison at the thought of it closing.

Here are eight takeaways from the gathering.

More than a half-dozen potential Democratic presidential candidates descended on Denver to make early pitches for themselves and their visions. They were not technically campaigning — at least not yet. But they were all eager to share how much they had to give to the country.

At one point on Friday, Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania was speaking on the main stage while Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan was taking questions from reporters. Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona was nearby, too, waiting to speak to the media.

Later, Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia gave a speech, then stayed to listen to Senator Cory Booker of New Jersey address the crowd. And Pete Buttigieg, the former transportation secretary, was sought after — especially after a rare nationwide ground stop was issued.

The pileup of hopefuls previewed what could be a crowded campaign.

The conference was hosted by Majority Democrats, a relatively new group that espouses a less ideological brand of Democratic politics and focuses on recruiting younger candidates. The group is funded chiefly by the hedge-fund billionaire Stephen Mandel and his wife, Sue. But billionaires still found themselves in the cross hairs of some progressives.

Representative Ro Khanna of California, who is considering a presidential run, called for a wealth tax on billionaires and accused Israel of a genocide to cheers.

Since Mr. Shapiro has rarely left Pennsylvania this year, his presence alone in Denver was notable. But on Friday, he spoke about his ambitions for the party — and his role in its future — both in his speech and an interview. He called it imperative for Democrats to construct a party that could win “370 electoral votes” — not just the 270 needed to win the presidency.

“We can’t be a party that is focused on sloganeering,” Mr. Shapiro said in an interview. “We have to be a party that’s focused on real deliverables.”

He said that the party can’t become “distracted by the shallow litmus test or trying to figure out where someone fits on some imaginary political spectrum.”

For many years, the Democratic presidential primary began in Iowa and New Hampshire, and then went to South Carolina. No longer.

In 2028, six early states will open the primary calendar: South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia.

Officials in Michigan, Virginia and New Mexico are already plotting how to take advantage of the new attention, circulating among ambitious Democrats on the sidelines of the conference.

For instance, Mr. Buttigieg ate Friday night with Don Scott, the House speaker in Virginia, which will hold the final primary before Super Tuesday. Mr. Scott said he told Mr. Buttigieg to start meeting with local leaders now if he wanted to be competitive in Virginia.

Shapiro. Gallego. Warnock. Booker. Khanna. Buttigieg.

Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois had aides and advisers circulating in Denver. So did Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky and Gov. Wes Moore of Maryland.

All those potential 2028 candidates — as well as Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, who was attending a climate summit in Turkey — are men.

Although women seem less certain to run, some could chase the Democratic nomination. That group includes former Vice President Kamala Harris, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and Ms. Slotkin, who gave the clearest indications yet that she was considering a run, saying in an interview that she was “seriously” weighing a bid.

Although she said that gender was not reason alone to run for the nation’s highest office, she added it was hard to ignore the possibility of the party being represented by only men in the primary.

“I would hate to see us go backwards by having no women enter the fray,” she said. Later, she said, “I know I want to be a part of the next generation that is helping to lead. That doesn’t necessarily mean I have to be the top dog.”

Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland arrived in Denver a day after declaring his underdog candidacy to unseat Senator Chuck Schumer of New York as the top Democrat in the Senate.

He received loud cheers when he restated his intention to the crowd, but Mr. Van Hollen is unlikely to succeed. One conference attendee came wearing a “Van Hollen For Leader” shirt modeled after the Van Halen logo but did not want to discuss on the record his support for the Maryland Democrat.

Mr. Van Hollen is an unlikely avatar of trying to upend the political status quo. He told reporters that he had “a record of running against the establishment,” while also noting in the same answer that he had served as chairman of both the House Democratic campaign arm and the Senate Democratic campaign arm.

“What has never changed about me is that I still believe we can support the underdog,” Mr. Van Hollen said.

In a small sign of frustration with the party’s old guard, Mr. Jeffries was repeatedly heckled while speaking onstage with Jessica Tarlov, a co-host of Fox News’s “The Five.” Mr. Jeffries waved off the hecklers dismissively by noting he was from Brooklyn.

“They didn’t win over a single person, but at least they got their clips for social,” Ms. Tarlov said afterward.

Ms. Slotkin said one of the most important qualities for a candidate in this media landscape was simply being compelling.

“The way citizens consume presidential elections is fundamentally changing,” she said. “I’m not sure we’ll ever have a boring president ever again.”

She just watched Abdul El-Sayed, a charismatic progressive, succeed in Michigan. And after a cycle in which a deluge of Republican cash failed to yield much return on the party’s investments, Democrats debated on the sidelines whether paid ads were as important as earning organic attention and riding the algorithm of social media.

“You can have all the great policy papers you want,” Ms. Slotkin said. “If you can’t convey authentically, that’s going to hold you back. And I think that’s actually OK.”

There was broad agreement among the could-be presidential candidates — and the Democrats who might work for them — that the time for choosing was near.

The competition for attention, donors and top staff is already steep. Many Democrats in Denver spoke of the relative dearth of top operatives who were eager to dedicate themselves to the rigors of a presidential primary campaign — especially with so many new Democratic congressional offices also staffing up.

Mr. Shapiro said he might announce his decision even before he tried to enact a robust agenda in the first 100 days with new Democratic state legislative majorities. Ms. Slotkin said she would decide early next year. And Mr. Warnock, who may have to choose between running for president and seeking Senate re-election in 2028, said nobody could dawdle.

“I don’t think there’s much time for anybody who thinks they want to do this,” he said.

item.title: Nvidia Fallout Looms Over Trump-Xi Meeting
item.description:
At major moments in President Trump’s second term, he has looked up during an economic speech or diplomatic dinner and asked a version of the same question: “Where’s Jensen?”

Jensen Huang has usually been out there, somewhere in the room.

Mr. Huang, who was until Thursday the leather-jacketed chief executive of Nvidia, one of the world’s largest companies, had impressed the president with his success, his money and his argument that keeping China dependent on American-made semiconductor chips and technology could help maintain U.S. dominance over Beijing.

Mr. Trump made sure to have the technology executive with him during pivotal U.S.-China meetings this year. The president invited him to come to China in May when he went to meet with Xi Jinping, China’s leader, stopping in Alaska, where Mr. Huang joined him on Air Force One at the last minute. And Mr. Huang was at the head table with the president when Mr. Trump hosted a state dinner for Mr. Xi at the White House in September.

But when Mr. Trump travels to China for another meeting with Mr. Xi at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation in Shenzhen this week, Mr. Huang, the man who has been influential in shaping the president’s views about technological competition with China, is not expected to be at his side.

Last week, Mr. Huang stepped down from his role at Nvidia after revelations that he had engaged in affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a woman who U.S. intelligence officials believe is an asset of Beijing.

Mr. Huang’s sudden fall and the U.S. finding that he was targeted by Chinese intelligence do not appear to have altered Mr. Trump’s estimation of the former Nvidia leader — or his approach to dealing with his Chinese counterpart in this week’s meeting. (Beijing has called the U.S. intelligence conclusions “smears and slanders.”)

So far, the president has not pressed Mr. Xi about his country’s espionage efforts or stepped in to resolve a raging debate within his administration about tightening export controls of A.I. technology and certain chips to China. Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, who has argued for less strict limits on chip exports to Asia, is expected to travel with him. In Shenzhen, Mr. Trump will participate in a meeting with Mr. Xi and, later, with Mr. Xi and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, in the first such gathering of the three leaders.

“Well, the big thing is, was the woman a spy?” Mr. Trump said in an interview with the podcaster and sports commentator Stephen A. Smith on Thursday, when asked if he thought Mr. Huang should have resigned. “And I don’t know if that’s been determined yet, but if the woman was a spy, yes. If the woman was not a spy, perhaps it would be different. But I can tell you this: Somehow, he’ll end up in his feet. I mean, I know him. I know him pretty well. I always thought of him as a fine man.”

Mr. Trump said last week that he did not plan to bring up the Nvidia matter with Mr. Xi but suggested that the Chinese leader could bring it up with him.

The president also said that he did not recall being briefed that Mr. Huang was in a close relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese executive believed by the United States to be a Chinese intelligence asset.

But Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Mr. Trump aboard Air Force One in May en route to China about the sensitive intelligence showing that Nvidia’s chief executive was in a relationship with the woman and that she was believed to be a Chinese spy, The New York Times reported last week. It was at least the second time the president was briefed on the intelligence, The Times reported.

Mr. Trump has continued to defend Mr. Huang, calling him an “honorable man” and questioning reports that he was briefed on the government’s intelligence findings.

“I’d have to check,” he told reporters last week in response to a question about when he first learned of the matter. “I’d certainly check with the intelligence people. They could have been mentioned. Certainly, it didn’t make much of an impact on me.”

The president’s blasé response to espionage allegations that have upended one of the world’s largest companies belies the economic and political storm caused by the revelations of Mr. Huang’s behavior. It also raises questions about how Mr. Trump would conduct himself during his meeting with Mr. Xi, an authoritarian leader whose friendship and admiration the president has courted.

“Trump has stood by Huang personally, and my read is that he sees espionage as something major powers just do to each other,” Craig Singleton, a China expert at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a nonpartisan think tank, said during a briefing last week. “He wants a very successful meeting and to show that he can manage the relationship with Xi Jinping.”

Indeed, Mr. Trump has said that espionage is the price of dealing with a powerful adversary. “You know what they say? That China spies on us. I say you’re right, and we spy on them, too,” he said in September.

White House officials said Friday that the Nvidia matter was a national security issue, and they did not expect the president to discuss it with Mr. Xi during their encounter.

In his two previous meetings this year with the Chinese leader, Mr. Trump showed little interest in extracting concessions from China.

Mr. Trump struck a conciliatory tone with Mr. Xi during his visit to Beijing in May, emphasizing their personal relationship. And when Mr. Xi visited Washington in the fall, weeks after Mr. Trump decried what he claimed was meddling by Beijing in the 2020 election, the president leaned into the pageantry of the occasion. The state visit produced little in terms of policy announcements on matters of tension between the two countries — on A.I., trade or the war in Iran.

But as Mr. Trump prepares to head to China again, Mr. Singleton noted that “the politics back in Washington are moving in a very different direction.”

The Trump administration is now facing questions and criticism over whether officials had properly policed the sale of chips to China. On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly blamed the Commerce Department for failing to curb the sale of advanced Nvidia technology to the Singaporean firm Megaspeed, which employed Ms. Huang and built data centers that provide computing power to Chinese companies.

“You will have to ask them about their internal processes,” he said of the Commerce Department, adding that his own agency had supported a stricter approach. “Treasury and my deputy has been pushing for this for months at the deputies level.”

Mr. Bessent has led the administration’s efforts to extend a trade truce with Beijing that expires in January. Despite continuing negotiations and the pause of a tit-for-tat trade war, administration officials remain frustrated with China’s restrictions on exports of crucial rare-earth metals and rare-earth magnets. Mr. Trump is expected to bring up that issue with Mr. Xi in Shenzhen.

While administration officials say the president will focus his meetings on rare-earth exports, nuclear proliferation and the war with Iran, Republicans and Democrats in Washington are demanding answers on Nvidia from Mr. Huang and Mr. Lutnick, who both have been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee in December.

“If Beijing was trying to keep American chips flowing, it may have helped build the bipartisan case for cutting that access off,” Mr. Singleton said.

It remains to be seen if that political pressure will force Mr. Trump to impose new restrictions on technology exports, or make another move that could constrain China.

Kenton Thibaut, a senior resident China fellow at the Atlantic Council, said that the Nvidia scandal was a “miserable” scenario for the Chinese, whose diplomatic aim with Mr. Trump is to placate him and keep a competitive relationship steady while reducing dependence on the economic choke points that Americans control.

“They wanted to keep this stasis in U.S.-China relations, prevent sort of any more export controls from coming into place, play nice with Trump and not rock the boat in any way,” Ms. Thibaut said. “And this is kind of like a disaster for them.”
